lessons.0.slides.0.description: Building a structured analytical framework for blind tasting
lessons.0.slides.1.title: The Purpose and Challenge of Blind Tasting
lessons.0.slides.1.content: Blind tasting is the ultimate test of wine expertise. With the label hidden, the taster must rely purely on their senses and knowledge to determine appellation, vintage, and producer. Burgundy blind tasting is particularly demanding: 36 villages, hundreds of individual parcels, subtle terroir differences. Mastering a systematic method is the key to success. A Master Sommelier must be able to blind-taste the region, village, and even specific parcel.
lessons.0.slides.2.title: 🔍 Systematic Blind Tasting Steps (Deductive Method)
lessons.0.slides.2.points.0: Sight: depth of colour, clarity, viscosity
lessons.0.slides.2.points.1: Nose: fruit, florals, spice, oak, age-related characteristics
lessons.0.slides.2.points.2: Palate: sweetness, acidity, tannins, body, flavour, finish
lessons.0.slides.2.points.4: Final assessment: appellation, vintage, quality level
lessons.0.slides.3.title: Beginner vs Expert Blind Tasting Approach
lessons.0.slides.4.title: Building a Sensory Memory Bank
lessons.0.slides.4.content: Blind tasting skill is built on an extensive sensory memory bank. You need to taste hundreds of wines and memorise the typical characteristics of each village: the power of Gevrey, the elegance of Chambolle, the floral complexity of Vosne. Record every tasting: the wine, colour, aromas, palate, impressions. Use tools like CellarTracker to track your tasting history. Over time, your brain forms 'terroir fingerprints' that let you identify a wine by smell and taste alone.
lessons.0.slides.5.title: 🎓 Master Blind Taster Training Progression (0→10 Years)
lessons.0.slides.6.title: 💡 Blind Tasting Training Tips
lessons.0.slides.6.points.0: Train weekly: fix 2–3 blind tasting sessions per week
lessons.0.slides.6.points.1: Easy to hard: first distinguish red from white, then village, then producer
lessons.0.slides.6.points.2: Double blind: no information of any kind
lessons.0.slides.6.points.3: Record and compare: reveal the answer after tasting and analyse differences
lessons.0.slides.6.points.4: Group discussion: share views with others and expand perspectives
lessons.0.slides.6.points.5: Set standards: taste at least 10 wines from each village before benchmarking

lessons.1.title: Village Character Identification
lessons.1.slides.0.title: Village Character Identification
lessons.1.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 2 - 17 min
lessons.1.slides.0.description: Mastering the terroir fingerprint of each village
lessons.1.slides.1.title: Terroir and Village Personality
lessons.1.slides.1.content: Every village in Burgundy has a unique 'personality', shaped by soil, microclimate, and winemaking tradition. Gevrey: powerful, structured, dark fruit, animale; Chambolle: elegant, silky, red fruit, floral; Vosne: spicy, rose-scented, deep, complex. Mastering these characteristics is the cornerstone of successful blind tasting.
lessons.1.slides.2.title: Gevrey vs Chambolle
lessons.1.slides.3.title: 🍷 Quick Profiles of Côte d'Or Villages
lessons.1.slides.3.points.0: Marsannay: light and fruity, easy-drinking, famous for rosé
lessons.1.slides.3.points.1: Fixin: firm structure, needs time, similar to Gevrey
lessons.1.slides.3.points.2: Morey-St-Denis: mineral, depth, between Gevrey and Chambolle
lessons.1.slides.3.points.4: Vougeot: highly variable (due to parcel diversity)
lessons.1.slides.4.title: Vosne vs Nuits-St-Georges
lessons.1.slides.5.title: White Wine Village Identification
lessons.1.slides.5.content: White wine identification also follows patterns: Meursault — hazelnut, butter, full body; Puligny — mineral, lemon, tight and elegant; Chassagne — between the two, almond, floral. Chablis with its distinctive marine minerality and high acidity is instantly recognisable. The power and ageing potential of Corton-Charlemagne are also unmistakable.

lessons.2.title: Vintage Identification Techniques
lessons.2.slides.0.title: Vintage Identification Techniques
lessons.2.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 3 - 16 min
lessons.2.slides.0.description: Determining vintage and maturity from the wine itself
lessons.2.slides.1.title: The Influence of Vintage
lessons.2.slides.1.content: Vintage determines grape ripeness, acidity, and tannin structure. Hot vintages (2015, 2018, 2019): deep colour, full body, low acidity, ripe fruit. Cool vintages (2014, 2016): paler colour, high acidity, elegant, mineral. Wet vintages (2011, 2013): diluted, rough tannins. Knowing vintage characteristics can dramatically improve blind tasting accuracy.
lessons.2.slides.2.title: Hot Vintage vs Cool Vintage
lessons.2.slides.3.title: 📅 Characteristics of Classic Vintages
lessons.2.slides.3.points.0: 2005: perfect balance, structure, longevity (drinking perfectly now)
lessons.2.slides.3.points.1: 2010: powerful, high acid, tannins (needs 5–10 more years)
lessons.2.slides.3.points.3: 2017: elegant, early-developing, fruity (in its prime now)
lessons.2.slides.4.title: Clues from Ageing
lessons.2.slides.4.content: As a wine ages, it shows signs of evolution: colour shifts from purple-red → brick-red → brown-amber; aromas develop from fruit → vegetal → animale; tannins evolve from raw → smooth → integrated. Under 5 years: fruit-driven, obvious tannins. 10–15 years: growing complexity, secondary aromas (forest floor, mushroom). 20+ years: tertiary aromas (leather, tobacco, earth), tannins fully integrated.
lessons.2.slides.5.title: 🌡️ Classic Vintage Climate and Style Comparison (2000–2020)
lessons.2.slides.6.title: 🕐 Stages of Ageing
lessons.2.slides.6.points.0: Youth (0–5 years): bright fruit, firm tannins, purple-red colour
lessons.2.slides.6.points.1: Development (5–10 years): fruit still present, beginning complexity, ruby colour
lessons.2.slides.6.points.2: Maturity (10–20 years): balance, complexity, brick-red with amber rim
lessons.2.slides.6.points.3: Peak (15–25 years): optimum condition, all elements in harmony
lessons.2.slides.6.points.4: Decline (25+ years): colour browning, aromas fading, still can be beautiful
lessons.2.slides.6.points.5: Key indicators: colour, freshness of fruit, state of tannins
lessons.2.slides.7.title: 💡 Vintage Identification Tips
lessons.2.slides.7.points.0: Learn vintage charts: memorise key vintage scores (2005=97, 2012=85)
lessons.2.slides.7.points.1: Climate knowledge: know whether the summer was hot or cool
lessons.2.slides.7.points.2: Cross-reference: hot vintage → high ripeness → high alcohol → full body
lessons.2.slides.7.points.3: Ageing estimate: colour + aroma type → estimate ageing time
lessons.2.slides.7.points.4: Process of elimination: can't be a hot vintage (pale colour, high acid)
lessons.2.slides.7.points.5: Conservative estimate: give a vintage range rather than a single year
lessons.2.slides.8.title: 🧠 Vintage Identification Technique Quiz
lessons.3.title: Producer Style Recognition
lessons.3.slides.0.title: Producer Style Recognition
lessons.3.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 4 - 17 min
lessons.3.slides.0.description: Identifying the winemaker's technique and philosophy
lessons.3.slides.1.title: How Producer Style Is Formed
lessons.3.slides.1.content: Even wines from the same parcel can be completely different depending on the producer. Winemaking philosophy (traditional vs modern), oak use (percentage of new barrels), extraction method (whole-cluster fermentation or not), and ageing time all leave a 'signature'. DRC's precise harmony, Leroy's dense power, Rousseau's classical elegance — all are recognisable.
lessons.3.slides.2.title: Traditional vs Modern Style
lessons.3.slides.3.title: 🏆 Signature Styles of Top Producers
lessons.3.slides.3.points.0: DRC: precise, harmonious, silky texture, long finish, extreme purity
lessons.3.slides.3.points.1: Leroy: concentrated, powerful, biodynamic, extremely low yield, explosive
lessons.3.slides.3.points.2: Rousseau: classical, elegant, mineral, long ageing potential, restrained
lessons.3.slides.3.points.3: Roumier: balanced, pure, clear fruit expression, moderate oak
lessons.3.slides.3.points.4: Dujac: whole-cluster fermentation, spice, elegance, drinks relatively early
lessons.3.slides.3.points.5: Méo-Camuzet: modern, polished, new oak, immediately seductive
lessons.3.slides.4.title: Clues from Oak
lessons.3.slides.4.content: New oak barrels impart vanilla, toast, mocha, and coconut aromas. Traditional producers use 20–30% new oak and it stays in the background; modern producers may use 100% new oak, with oak prominently apparent. In blind tasting, overly obvious oak often points to a modern-style or New World producer. In top Burgundy, oak should be seamlessly integrated, never overpowering the fruit.
lessons.3.slides.5.title: 🏆 Evolution of Legendary Burgundy Domaine Styles (1920s→2026)
lessons.3.slides.6.title: 🔍 Methods for Identifying Producers
lessons.3.slides.6.points.0: Oak level: proportion of new barrels reflects style (high = modern)
lessons.3.slides.6.points.2: Extraction intensity: deep and concentrated (Leroy) vs pale and elegant (Rousseau)
lessons.3.slides.6.points.3: Purity: extreme purity usually signals a top estate
lessons.3.slides.6.points.4: Complexity: layered complexity implies old vines and low yields
lessons.3.slides.6.points.5: Consistency: unwavering style year after year is a hallmark of great estates
lessons.3.slides.7.title: 💡 Advanced Identification Techniques
lessons.3.slides.7.points.0: Build a reference library: taste multiple vintages from the same producer
lessons.3.slides.7.points.1: Horizontal comparison: blind taste different producers from the same vintage
lessons.3.slides.7.points.2: Record characteristics: note the 'signature elements' of each producer
lessons.3.slides.7.points.3: Group blind tasting: hear others' views to expand your understanding
lessons.3.slides.7.points.4: Focus on the top ten: master the styles of the top 10 estates first
lessons.3.slides.7.points.5: Stay humble: producer identification is the hardest; don't be overconfident
lessons.3.slides.8.title: 🧠 Producer Style Identification Quiz
lessons.4.title: Assessing the Stage of Ageing
lessons.4.slides.0.title: Assessing the Stage of Ageing
lessons.4.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 5 - 16 min
lessons.4.slides.0.description: Evaluating a wine's maturity and drinking window
lessons.4.slides.1.title: Understanding the Ageing Curve
lessons.4.slides.1.content: A wine's life cycle follows a parabolic arc: youth (closed, raw tannins) → development (beginning to show complexity) → peak (all elements in perfect balance) → decline (fruit fading, acidity prominent). Top Burgundy can sustain its peak for 10–15 years before a gradual decline. Assessing the stage of ageing helps decide when to drink or sell.
lessons.4.slides.2.title: 🔴 Red Wine Ageing Characteristics
lessons.4.slides.2.points.0: 0–3 years: deep purple-red, bright fruit, firm tannins, closed
lessons.4.slides.2.points.1: 3–8 years: ruby, fruit and oak integrating, tannins softening
lessons.4.slides.2.points.2: 8–15 years: garnet, secondary aromas emerging (forest floor, mushroom)
lessons.4.slides.2.points.3: 15–25 years: brick-red, tertiary aromas (leather, tobacco), silky
lessons.4.slides.2.points.4: 25+ years: amber-tinged rim, fruit faint, animale and earth dominant
lessons.4.slides.2.points.5: Assessment: colour + aroma type + tannin texture
lessons.4.slides.3.title: Young vs Aged Wine
lessons.4.slides.4.title: White Wine Ageing Characteristics
lessons.4.slides.4.content: Burgundy whites also follow a pattern: young (0–5 years) — bright gold, citrus lemon, high acidity; mature (8–15 years) — deep gold, hazelnut and honey, creamy texture; old (20+ years) — amber, caramel and truffle, notes of oxidation. Top Chablis Grand Crus can age 30+ years; Meursault matures relatively faster.
lessons.4.slides.5.title: 🔴 Complete Visual of Red Wine Ageing Evolution (2005 Grand Cru Tracking)
lessons.4.slides.6.title: ⚪ Stages of White Wine Ageing
lessons.4.slides.6.points.0: 0–3 years: pale lemon, bright citrus, high acidity, mineral
lessons.4.slides.6.points.1: 3–8 years: gold, hazelnut emerging, creamy texture, growing complexity
lessons.4.slides.6.points.2: 8–15 years: deep gold, honey, roasted almond, rich and round
lessons.4.slides.6.points.3: 15+ years: amber, caramel, truffle, oxidative aromas (good examples)
lessons.4.slides.6.points.5: White wines are fragile: easier to over-age than reds
lessons.4.slides.7.title: 💡 Practical Ageing Assessment
lessons.4.slides.7.points.0: Colour is the guide: purple-red → garnet → brick-red → brown (sequential ageing)
lessons.4.slides.7.points.1: Aroma evolution: fruit → floral → vegetal → animale → earth
lessons.4.slides.7.points.2: Tannin texture: rough → fine → silky → absent
lessons.4.slides.7.points.3: Fruit freshness: full → diminishing → faint → gone
lessons.4.slides.7.points.4: Complexity development: simple → complex → at its peak → declining
lessons.4.slides.7.points.5: Drinking advice: use stage assessment to decide whether to drink immediately
lessons.4.slides.8.title: 🧠 Ageing Assessment and Drinking Window Quiz
lessons.5.title: Writing Professional Tasting Notes
lessons.5.slides.0.title: Writing Professional Tasting Notes
lessons.5.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 6 - 16 min
lessons.5.slides.0.description: Writing clear, accurate, and professional tasting reports
lessons.5.slides.1.title: The Importance of Tasting Notes
lessons.5.slides.1.content: Professional tasting notes are not only personal records but also tools for communicating with others. Good notes should be: accurate description, clear structure, reproducible, avoiding subjective bias. Scores and notes from authorities like Wine Advocate and Wine Spectator influence market prices. Mastering professional terminology and writing conventions is an essential skill for any professional taster.
lessons.5.slides.2.title: 📝 Tasting Note Structure (Standard Format)
lessons.5.slides.2.points.2: Aroma description: fruit, florals, spice, oak, other
lessons.5.slides.2.points.3: Palate: sweetness, acidity, tannins, body, flavour, finish
lessons.5.slides.2.points.4: Balance and complexity: are elements harmonious? How many layers?
lessons.5.slides.2.points.5: Conclusion: quality rating, drinking advice, ageing potential
lessons.5.slides.3.title: Amateur vs Professional Notes
lessons.5.slides.4.title: 🎓 Professional Sommelier Career Development Path (0→15 Years)
lessons.5.slides.5.title: Vocabulary Bank
lessons.5.slides.5.content: Professional tasting requires rich vocabulary: fruit (red cherry, blackberry, raspberry, blackcurrant), florals (violet, rose, peony), spice (cinnamon, clove, pepper), oak (vanilla, toast, cedar), earth (forest floor, mushroom, wet stone), animale (leather, meat, musk). Avoid overly obscure descriptors — aim for objectivity and clarity.
lessons.5.slides.6.title: 🎯 Use of Professional Terminology
lessons.5.slides.6.points.0: Acidity: low, medium−, medium, medium+, high
lessons.5.slides.6.points.1: Tannins: soft, silky, fine-grained, grainy, grippy, harsh
lessons.5.slides.6.points.3: Finish: short (<3 sec), medium (3–5 sec), long (>5 sec)
lessons.5.slides.6.points.4: Complexity: simple, moderate, complex, very complex
lessons.5.slides.7.title: 📊 Scoring Systems
lessons.5.slides.7.points.3: Recommended: use the 100-point scale, most universally understood
lessons.5.slides.7.points.4: Scoring criteria: balance, complexity, ageing potential, typicity
lessons.5.slides.7.points.5: Score carefully: don't give 95+ lightly; reserve for the truly exceptional
lessons.5.slides.8.title: 💡 Practical Writing Tips
lessons.5.slides.8.points.0: Record immediately: write notes during tasting, not from memory later
lessons.5.slides.8.points.1: Use a template: consistent format ensures nothing is missed
lessons.5.slides.8.points.2: Objective first: describe objectively before offering subjective opinion
lessons.5.slides.8.points.3: Avoid bias: don't let an estate's reputation influence your description
lessons.5.slides.8.points.4: Continuous revision: after revealing the answer, reflect and refine your sensory memory
lessons.5.slides.8.points.5: Go digital: use apps like CellarTracker and Vivino to record notes
